cases.note: c+ check rejects this constant OOB statically, but this runner uses plain clang and only sees a raw SIGSEGV; UBSan would also report it if enabled.
The volatile OOB read is silent under plain clang; only UBSan reports it, and no checked API covers a raw stack subscript.
Both refuse the oversized request by design; this is genuine safe handling, not a proof about arbitrary raw allocations.
C detects only allocator-tracked stale aliases via the recent-free cache; an alias whose address was re-issued is not provably distinguishable, and Rust rejects at compile time.
free_checked_s catches a second release through a bounded recent-free cache; raw free(p) twice stays UB and is not UBSan-detectable.
Escaped stack addresses are a documented C+ compiler gap; the stale read prints a value and exits 0, so nothing proves safety here.
The guarded C API rejects NULL with EINVAL, but unguarded raw NULL dereference remains UB; Rust rejects the type mismatch instead.
The unsynchronised C increment silently loses updates; only ThreadSanitizer would detect it, and C+ metadata locking does not cover caller state.
size_t wrapping is defined so UBSan does not flag it; C detects the resulting allocation-count mismatch via metadata, while rustc rejects the constant overflow.
The uninitialized struct field reads an indeterminate value and exits 0; neither C+, -Wuninitialized nor UBSan diagnoses this shape.

C validates the index only because the heap table has tracked length metadata; a raw stack table with a wrong length cannot be validated, and Rust panics on the runtime index. [updated to measured rustc 1.100.0 behaviour: this case is rejected at compile time]

Neither language enforces the external contract: C crashes on the NULL argument, and Rust's unsafe marker only shifts responsibility to the caller before its null check aborts. [updated to measured rustc 1.100.0 behaviour: this case is rejected at compile time]
